newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't sounds upbeat in re-election run-up.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't sounds upbeat in re-election run-up.

text.p: The Brazilian government, sounding confident it had cracked opposition to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election plan, said this week's scheduled vote on a re-election bill would go ahead.

Government whips said they expected between 330 and 340 votes in favour of the bill when it is put to a first of two votes on the floor of the Chamber of Deputies on either Tuesday evening or Wednesday afternoon.
As a constitutional amendment, the bill requires two three-fifths majorities, each equivalent to 308 votes, before moving on to the Senate.

Deputy Benito Gama, the government's leader in the lower house, said opposition to the timing of the re-election vote within the normally Cardoso-allied Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) had been largely overcome.
"We will have to wait to see the result but we are certain the vast majority of the PMDB will vote in favor of re-election," Gama told national CBN Radio.
The PMDB is the largest party in Congress with 102 of a total 513 votes in the Chamber of Deputies.

It dashed the government's plan to approve re-election in the lower house in January when a convention insisted the party only vote on re-election after elections in early February for the new presidents of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

Cardoso spent last week meeting with deputies from the PMDB and other parties in a bid to muster the necessary support for the re-election bill and seemed to have clinched the support of powerful PMDB senator and former president Jose Sarney.

News reports over the weekend said Sarney, in his last weeks as president of the Senate, met with Cardoso on Friday and afterwards told friends the re-election bill would be approved in the lower house vote.

But the government were taking no chances. Whips were asking deputies who own private jets to make them available for a few lawmakers who were sick or in hospital and might not otherwise attend Brasilia this week.
The government also hoped a rally of recently elected mayors in favor of re-election in Congress on Tuesday would help convince deputies who have not yet made up their minds how or whether to vote.
Mayors and state governors stand to win the right to stand for a second, along with presidents, under the terms of the re-election amendment .
"There are still last minute talks and we're counting the numbers to make sure people are going to be around," said a government source in Congress who asked not to be identified.
